claim: Mouse yolk sac visceral endoderm (VE) cells have huge endocytic vesicles.
source: VE cells play a critical role in the maternofetal exchange of nutrients before the establishment of a chorioallantoic placenta: they vigorously endocytose maternal proteins, hydrolyze the proteins in lysosomes, and supply the resultant products to the developing embryo (Bielinska et al., 1999; Jollie, 1990). Reflecting this high endocytic activity, VE cells are characterized by huge endosomal vesicles (Bielinska et al., 1999; Kawamura et al., 2012; Koike et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature describing VE cell characteristics

claim: Late endosomes of VE cells exhibit two distinct modes of fusion: homotypic fusion with late endosomes in an explosive fusion-like manner and heterotypic fusion with lysosomes in a bridge fusion-like manner.
source: Here, we show that late endosomes of VE cells exhibit different modes of fusion with target organelles depending on their targets: they undergo homotypic fusion with late endosomes in an explosive fusion-like manner and heterotypic fusion with lysosomes in a bridge fusion-like manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and introduction, supported by experimental observations described in the Results section

claim: Vesicle size is a critical determinant of fusion types.
source: Mathematical modeling showed that vesicle size is a critical determinant of these fusion types and that membrane fluctuation forces can overcome the vesicle size effects.
evidence: Supported by mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript

claim: Membrane fluctuation forces can overcome vesicle size effects on fusion type.
source: Mathematical modeling showed that vesicle size is a critical determinant of these fusion types and that membrane fluctuation forces can overcome the vesicle size effects.
evidence: Supported by mathematical modeling results and experimental data with actin inhibitors

claim: Actin filaments are bound to late endosomes in VE cells.
source: We found that actin filaments were bound to late endosomes and forces derived from dynamic actin remodeling were necessary for quick fusion during homotypic fusion.
evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining and microscopy data shown in Figure 5

claim: Forces derived from dynamic actin remodeling are necessary for quick fusion during homotypic fusion.
source: We found that actin filaments were bound to late endosomes and forces derived from dynamic actin remodeling were necessary for quick fusion during homotypic fusion.
evidence: Supported by experiments with cytochalasin D and jasplakinolide showing altered fusion dynamics

claim: Cofilin plays a role in endocytic fusion by regulating actin turnover.
source: Furthermore, cofilin played a role in endocytic fusion by regulating actin turnover.
evidence: Supported by experiments with S3 peptide (cofilin activator) showing effects on fusion frequency and actin dynamics

claim: Actin promotes vesicle fusion for efficient membrane trafficking in visceral endoderm cells.
source: These data suggest that actin promotes vesicle fusion for efficient membrane trafficking in visceral endoderm cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing actin's role in fusion

claim: Different types of endosomal vesicles are aligned from the apical to the basal area in the supranuclear portion of VE cells.
source: These observations revealed that different types of endosomal vesicles were aligned from the apical to the basal area in the supranuclear portion of VE cells, reflecting the repeated fusion and enlargement of vesicles as they migrated deeper into the cell (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy observations and organelle marker staining shown in Figure 1

claim: Small vesicles in zone 1 (within 0.5-1 μm of the apical surface) are positive for EEA1, indicating they are early endosomes.
source: In the most superficial portion (within 0.5–1 μm of the apical surface; designated as zone 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), fuzzy FM1-43 staining was observed (Figure 1B). The small vesicles in this zone were positive for EEA1 (Figure 1B), indicating that they were early endosomes.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data with EEA1 antibody shown in Figure 1B

claim: Medium-sized round vesicles in zone 2 (at a depth of 1-6 μm from the apical surface) are positive for Rab7, suggesting they are late endosomes.
source: Immediately beneath zone 1, many medium-sized round vesicles were observed (zone 2; at a depth of 1–6 μm from the apical surface, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). Electroporation of EGFP-Rab7 revealed that these vesicles were positive for Rab7, suggesting that they were late endosomes.
evidence: Supported by EGFP-Rab7 expression data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Large amorphous lysosomes in zone 3 (at a depth of 6-16 μm from the apical surface) are positive for LysoTracker Red and LAMP1.
source: In the deep portion (zone 3; at a depth of 6–16 μm from the apical surface, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), large amorphous lysosomes, positive for LysoTracker Red and LAMP1, were observed (Figure 1B; Koike et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by LysoTracker Red staining and LAMP1 immunostaining shown in Figure 1B

claim: Endocytosed transferrin is rapidly transported from early endosomes to lysosomes via late endosomes in VE cells.
source: The time course of the numbers of labeled vesicles in each zone showed that endocytosed transferrin was rapidly transported from early endosomes to lysosomes via late endosomes in VE cells, as reported previously (Richardson et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging of Alexa 488-transferrin shown in Figure 1D and E

claim: In homotypic fusion, two late endosomes fuse quickly in an explosive mode where a membrane pore quickly expands.
source: First, from 5 min after pulse labeling, fusion of two neighboring late endosomes was observed frequently (Figure 2A and B; Video 1). The fusion showed an explosive mode, in which a membrane pore quickly expanded and two vesicles fused to become a single vesicle (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2 and Video 1

claim: Homotypic fusion is completed within 20-50 seconds (mean 31.9±0.2 s, n=37).
source: The fusion was completed within 20–50 s (the time required from membrane fusion to single spherical vesicle formation was 31.9±0.2 s, n=37), and the time was weakly correlated with the vesicle size (r=0.60, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The time required for homotypic fusion completion is weakly correlated with vesicle size (r=0.60).
source: The fusion was completed within 20–50 s (the time required from membrane fusion to single spherical vesicle formation was 31.9±0.2 s, n=37), and the time was weakly correlated with the vesicle size (r=0.60, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: Late endosomes of any size undergo homotypic fusion.
source: The size distribution of the late endosomes that underwent fusion (7.3±6.6 μm2, n=34) was similar to that of the total late endosomes in the observed area at the start of recording (5.7±6.4 μm2, n=265; Figure 2C), indicating that late endosomes of any size underwent homotypic fusion.
evidence: Supported by size distribution analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: Heterotypic fusion between late endosomes and lysosomes occurs as bridge fusion where the pore does not expand and the late endosome gradually shrinks.
source: Second, from 15 min after pulse labeling, some late endosomes shrank gradually and disappeared from the focal plane (Figure 3A and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3 and Video 2

claim: The disappearance of late endosomes is a consequence of fusion with underlying lysosomes, not engulfment, in E8.5 embryos.
source: These data suggest that the disappearance of late endosomes is a consequence of fusion with the underlying lysosomes, but not of engulfment in E8.5 embryos.
evidence: Supported by differential labeling experiments and electron microscopy showing pore formation between late endosomes and lysosomes

claim: Heterotypic fusion is slower than homotypic fusion and is completed within 90-250 seconds (mean 154.8±1.4 s, n=25).
source: This type of fusion, so-called bridge fusion, described in a previous study (Nicot et al., 2006; Roberts et al., 1999), occurred as a result of the slow mixing of vesicular contents through a narrow fusion pore. Actually, heterotypic fusion was slower than homotypic fusion and was completed within 90–250 s (154.8±1.4 s, n=25), and the fusion time (the time required from membrane fusion to disappearance of the vesicle) did not correlate with the vesicle size (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3F

claim: The fusion time in heterotypic fusion does not correlate with vesicle size.
source: Actually, heterotypic fusion was slower than homotypic fusion and was completed within 90–250 s (154.8±1.4 s, n=25), and the fusion time (the time required from membrane fusion to disappearance of the vesicle) did not correlate with the vesicle size (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3F

claim: Larger late endosomes tend to undergo heterotypic fusion.
source: The size of the labeled late endosomes at this time point (10.1±8.1 μm2, n=256) was larger than that at 5 min after labeling (6.7±6.2 μm2, n=242), indicating that larger late endosomes tended to undergo heterotypic fusion (Figure 3G, see also below).
evidence: Supported by size distribution analysis at different time points shown in Figure 3G

claim: The size of late endosomes is not the sole trigger for heterotypic fusion.
source: However, the size of the late endosomes that underwent heterotypic fusion (10.2±9.2 μm2, n=34) did not differ from that of the total late endosomes at 15 min after labeling (Figure 3G), indicating that the size of late endosomes is not the sole trigger for heterotypic fusion.
evidence: Supported by size distribution comparison shown in Figure 3G

claim: The free energy of a vesicle consists of bending energy and osmotic energy.
source: According to thermodynamics, the deformation of a physical object proceeds as its free energy decreases. The free energy of a vesicle consists of two terms: bending energy and osmotic energy.
evidence: This is based on established thermodynamic principles applied to vesicle systems

claim: Vesicle size intrinsically affects the balance of bending energy and osmotic energy and may be a critical factor for membrane deformation during fusion.
source: Note that the bending energy depends only on its shape; in other words, two membranes with the same shape but with different sizes have the same bending energy. On the other hand, the volume depends on both the size and the shape. Therefore, the vesicle size intrinsically affects the balance of both energy sources and may be a critical factor for membrane deformation during fusion.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference from the mathematical model

claim: Mathematical modeling predicts that late endosomes are large enough to allow bridge fusion to occur, although they exhibit explosive fusion in vivo.
source: Our modeling predicted that the late endosomes are large enough to allow bridge fusion to occur, although they exhibit explosive fusion in vivo.
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical model that contrasts with experimental observations

claim: Membrane fluctuation is a critical factor determining fusion mode beyond vesicle size.
source: These observations indicate that vesicle size is not the sole factor determining the fusion mode. Lipid composition, a well-known parameter affecting its bending modulus, is also involved, but the effect on fusion mode may be less dominant when compared with the vesicle size effects (Simson et al., 1998; Faizi et al., 2019; Ridolfi et al., 2021). One of the critical factors other than vesicle size that determine the fusion mode is membrane fluctuation.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between model predictions and experimental observations, supported by citations

claim: Homotypic fusion is converted to bridge-like fusion after cytochalasin D treatment.
source: We found that homotypic fusion was converted to bridge-like fusion after cytochalasin D treatment (Figure 7C), which suggests that actin dynamics around vesicles cause fluctuation and affect the fusion modes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with cytochalasin D shown in Figure 7C

claim: Actin dynamics around vesicles cause fluctuation and affect fusion modes.
source: We found that homotypic fusion was converted to bridge-like fusion after cytochalasin D treatment (Figure 7C), which suggests that actin dynamics around vesicles cause fluctuation and affect the fusion modes.
evidence: This is inferred from the cytochalasin D experimental results

claim: A larger fluctuation can shift the fusion mode from bridge to explosive fusion.
source: This finding can be successfully explained by introducing minor modifications in our mathematical modeling so that a larger fluctuation can shift the fusion mode from bridge to explosive fusion.
evidence: Supported by Monte Carlo simulations shown in Figure 4F

claim: VE cells vigorously endocytose maternal proteins and supply digested products to the developing embryo to support embryonic development.
source: VE cells vigorously endocytose maternal proteins and supply the digested products to the developing embryo to support embryonic development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VE cell function

claim: Larger vesicle size leads to reduction in vesicle fusion speed and subsequent nutrient trafficking efficiency.
source: However, larger vesicle size leads to the reduction in the vesicle fusion speed and subsequent nutrient trafficking efficiency.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the relationship between vesicle size and fusion dynamics

claim: Forces generated by actin increase the rate of vesicular trafficking and overcome the disadvantage of large vesicle size.
source: If vesicle size were the only factor determining the fusion mode, this disadvantage would occur, but if fluctuation is taken into account, it can be overcome, as shown in our mathematical modeling, and the forces generated by actin are thought to be responsible for increasing the rate of vesicular trafficking.
evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical modeling and experimental results

claim: Knockout mice of actin-related genes (Arc and Myh9) show abnormal VE cells and embryonic lethality.
source: This idea is supported by previous reports that knockout mice of actin-related genes (e.g. Arc and Myh9) showed abnormal VE cells and embryonic lethality (Conti et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: In heterotypic fusion, lysosomes are too large compared to late endosomes and actin accumulation on lysosomal membrane is scarce, resulting in insufficient force for explosive fusion.
source: In heterotypic fusion, late endosomes fused with lysosomes in a bridge-like manner. This may be because lysosomes are too large in comparison with late endosomes and actin accumulation on the lysosomal membrane is scarce, resulting in insufficient force of actin for explosive fusion.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed heterotypic fusion mode

claim: Two types of actin filaments are associated with late endosomes in VE cells: those extending along the apical-basal axis and those extending radially from the endosomes.
source: We found two types of actin filaments associated with late endosomes in VE cells: those that extended along the apical-basal axis and those that extended radially from the endosomes (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by high-resolution imaging data shown in Figure 5

claim: Strong actin signals are detected associated with the cell membrane in VE cells.
source: In VE cells, strong signals were detected to be associated with the cell membrane (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining shown in Figure 5A-C

claim: Small punctates and short filaments of actin are detected in the cytoplasm in zone 2 and are bound to the surface of late endosomes.
source: In zone 2, small punctates and short filaments were detected in the cytoplasm (Figure 5B) and were bound to the surface of late endosomes (Figure 5B, B' and B'') and infrequently to lysosomes in zone 3 (Figure 5C, C' and C'').
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 5B and 5C

claim: Several rod-like actin filaments extend from the apical side of VE cells into the cytoplasm and surround and hold late endosomes.
source: Optical cross-sectional images and 3D reconstruction showed that several rod-like actin filaments, extending from the apical side of VE cells into the cytoplasm, surrounded and held the late endosomes (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Supported by 3D reconstruction images shown in Figure 5D-F

claim: Most actin punctates observed in the x-y plane correspond to cross-sectional images of actin filaments extending in the apical-to-basal direction.
source: These data indicate that most actin punctates observed in the x-y plane correspond to the cross-sectional images of actin filaments extending in the apical-to-basal direction.
evidence: This is inferred from the 3D reconstruction data

claim: Most actin punctates surrounding late endosomes are bundled.
source: In addition, when a fusion protein of an actin-bundling protein, fascin-1, with a red fluorescent protein was expressed in VE cells by electroporation, fascin-1 was highly colocalized with the actin punctates, suggesting that most of the actin punctates surrounding the late endosomes were bundled (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by fascin-1 colocalization data shown in Figure 5G

claim: Fine actin filaments extend radially from endosomal membranes in the x-y plane.
source: To investigate the endosome-associated actin filaments in more detail, we performed high-resolution imaging analysis using a deconvolution technique, which had resolution comparable to super-resolution microscopy. It demonstrated that fine actin filaments extended radially from the endosomal membranes in the x-y plane, in addition to the actin filaments extending in the apical-basal axis (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by deconvolution microscopy images shown in Figure 5H

claim: Actin turnover on the surface of late endosomes is dynamically regulated, with a tendency to be more active in the apical area than in the basal area.
source: These results indicated that actin turnover on the surface of late endosomes was dynamically regulated, with a tendency to be more active in the apical area than in the basal area.
evidence: Supported by FRAP assay data showing different recovery times in apical vs basal regions (Figure 6C-E)

claim: When late endosomes move in the x-y plane in zone 2, spots of EGFP-actin are always at the rear-end of the endosomes along the moving direction.
source: The time-lapse images showed that when late endosomes moved in an x-y plane in zone 2, spots of EGFP-actin were always at the rear-end of the endosomes along the moving direction (Figure 6F, n=13).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization on the membrane acts as the driving force of motility of intracellular pathogens and endosomes/lysosomes in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Because it is known that Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization on the membrane acts as the driving force of the motility of intracellular pathogens (Welch and Way, 2013) and endosomes/lysosomes in Xenopus egg extracts (Taunton et al., 2000), we examined the localization of Arp2/3 in VE cells to test the possible role of Arp2/3 in endosome migration.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Arp3-EGFP signals are distributed in dots on late endosomes and partially colocalize with phalloidin spots in the x-y plane in zone 2.
source: When a fusion protein of Arp3-EGFP was expressed in VE cells by electroporation, the EGFP signals were distributed in dots on the late endosomes and partially colocalized with phalloidin spots in the x-y plane in zone 2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Arp3-EGFP localization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: Arp3-EGFP signals are always seen at the rear-end of endosomes along the moving direction.
source: In addition, Arp3-EGFP signals were always seen at the rear-end of the endosomes along the moving direction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: Radial branched filaments are temporally polymerized to provide propulsive force on the membrane for intracellular movement.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the radial branched filaments are temporally polymerized to provide the propulsive force on the membrane for intracellular movement.
evidence: This is inferred from the Arp3 localization and actin dynamics data

claim: Treatment with cytochalasin D reduces the frequency of homotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Treatment with cytochalasin D (a cell-permeable inhibitor of actin polymerization) for 5 min significantly changed the distribution of actin filaments. High-resolution imaging analysis using a deconvolution technique showed that phalloidin-positive filamentous structures decreased and instead actin aggregation was observed in the cytosol (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). The treatment reduced the frequency of homotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7A and B; Video 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with cytochalasin D shown in Figure 7A and B

claim: Treatment with 0.1 or 1.0 μM cytochalasin D slows down homotypic fusion.
source: In addition, it altered the speed and mode of the fusion. Treatment with 0.1 or 1.0 μM cytochalasin D slowed down homotypic fusion (Figure 7C and D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7C and D

claim: Upon 1.0 μM cytochalasin D treatment, about one-third of homotypic fusion shows bridge fusion.
source: Furthermore, upon 1.0 μM cytochalasin D treatment, about one-third of homotypic fusion showed bridge fusion (Figure 7C and E; Video 4).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7C and E

claim: Cytochalasin D slows down fusion processes and changes the fusion mode to bridge fusion at higher concentrations.
source: Therefore, cytochalasin D slowed down the fusion processes and changed the fusion mode to bridge fusion at higher concentrations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the cytochalasin D experimental results

claim: Treatment with jasplakinolide reduces the frequency of homotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Treatment with jasplakinolide (a cell-permeable stabilizer of actin filaments) also changed the actin dynamics. After the treatment, the actin meshwork beneath the plasma membrane (zone 1) was denser (Figure 7—figure supplement 2). Furthermore, actin filaments extending radially from the late endosomes were thicker and the fluorescence intensity was increased, although the actin filaments extending from the apical-basal axis were not changed (Figure 7—figure supplement 2). The treatment reduced the frequency of homotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7A and B; Video 5), indicating that dynamic actin turnover is required for homotypic fusion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with jasplakinolide shown in Figure 7A and B

claim: Dynamic actin turnover is required for homotypic fusion.
source: The treatment reduced the frequency of homotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7A and B; Video 5), indicating that dynamic actin turnover is required for homotypic fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the jasplakinolide experimental results

claim: When late endosomes undergo fusion, EGFP-actin punctates are excluded from membrane docking sites and highly polymerized transiently at both ends of fusing vesicles during the rounding period.
source: We next observed the distribution of actin filaments during homotypic fusion. When late endosomes underwent fusion, EGFP-actin punctates were excluded from the membrane docking sites and highly polymerized transiently at both ends of the fusing vesicles (opposite to the docking region) during the rounding period after membrane fusion (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging of EGFP-actin during fusion shown in Figure 7F

claim: Actin filament distribution is spatially regulated during fusion.
source: The fluorescence intensity of EGFP-actin on endosomes was quantitated in the proximal, lateral, and distal regions at the predocking, docking, rounding, and postfusion stages. This analysis indicated that actin filament distribution was spatially regulated during fusion (Figure 7G, dark gray bar), whereas FM 1–43 distribution, used as an unchanged control, was uniform on the membrane throughout the rounding stages (Figure 7G, light gray bar).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of EGFP-actin distribution shown in Figure 7G

claim: The total fluorescence intensity of EGFP-actin on late endosomes significantly increases transiently after pore formation.
source: Furthermore, the total fluorescence intensity of EGFP-actin on late endosomes significantly increased transiently after pore formation (Figure 7H), indicating that actin filaments were polymerized temporarily, not simply distributed differently.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7H

claim: Actin filaments are polymerized temporarily during fusion, not simply distributed differently.
source: Furthermore, the total fluorescence intensity of EGFP-actin on late endosomes significantly increased transiently after pore formation (Figure 7H), indicating that actin filaments were polymerized temporarily, not simply distributed differently.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in total EGFP-actin fluorescence intensity

claim: Treatment with CK-666 (an Arp2/3 inhibitor) results in a decrease in the frequency of homotypic fusion and slows down homotypic fusion.
source: Moreover, accumulation of Arp3-EGFP in the distal region during the rounding stage was observed similarly to EGFP-actin accumulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 4), and treatment with CK-666, an Arp2/3 inhibitor, resulted in a decrease in the frequency of homotypic fusion (Figure 7B) and slowed down homotypic fusion (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with CK-666 shown in Figure 7B, C, and D

claim: Branched actin filaments nucleated by the Arp2/3 complex on the distal surface of late endosomes are necessary to transform the vesicle into a large round sphere quickly after membrane fusion.
source: These results suggest that branched actin filaments nucleated by the Arp2/3 complex on the distal surface of late endosomes are necessary to transform the vesicle into a large round sphere quickly after membrane fusion of late endosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the Arp3 localization and CK-666 inhibition data

claim: Cytochalasin D treatment leads to a significant reduction in the frequency of heterotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We next examined the role of actin filaments in heterotypic fusion. Cytochalasin D treatment led to a significant reduction in the frequency of heterotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 8A–C and Video 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with cytochalasin D shown in Figure 8A-C

claim: Jasplakinolide treatment does not inhibit heterotypic fusion and increases the frequency of heterotypic fusion with lysosomes at 5 min after pulse labeling.
source: In contrast, jasplakinolide treatment did not inhibit heterotypic fusion and somehow increased the frequency of heterotypic fusion with lysosomes at as early as 5 min after pulse labeling (Figure 8B and Video 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with jasplakinolide shown in Figure 8B

claim: CK-666 treatment has no effects on heterotypic fusion, suggesting that Arp2/3 is not required for heterotypic fusion.
source: In addition, CK-666 treatment had no effects, suggesting that Arp2/3 was not required for heterotypic fusion (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with CK-666 shown in Figure 8C

claim: Actin plays distinct roles in homotypic fusion and heterotypic fusion.
source: These data suggest that actin played distinct roles in homotypic fusion and heterotypic fusion and that stable actin filaments are implicated in driving heterotypic fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of actin inhibitors on the two fusion types

claim: Stable actin filaments are implicated in driving heterotypic fusion.
source: These data suggest that actin played distinct roles in homotypic fusion and heterotypic fusion and that stable actin filaments are implicated in driving heterotypic fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the jasplakinolide results showing increased heterotypic fusion

claim: Heterotypic fusion frequency is reduced to 20% by MyoVin-1 (myosin V inhibitor) and to a lesser extent by blebbistatin (NM II inhibitor).
source: Heterotypic fusion frequency was reduced to 20% by MyoVin-1 and to a lesser extent, but significantly, by blebbistatin, but was not affected by PClP or TIP (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with myosin inhibitors shown in Figure 8D

claim: Homotypic fusion frequency is significantly reduced by PClP (myosin I inhibitor), MyoVin-1 (myosin V inhibitor), and TIP (myosin VI inhibitor).
source: In contrast, homotypic fusion frequency was significantly reduced by PClP, MyoVin-1, and TIP (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with myosin inhibitors shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: EGFP-myosin IIA signals overlap with phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes.
source: EGFP-myosin IIA signals overlapped with phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes (Figure 8E), whereas EGFP-myosin Va signals were juxtaposed to phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 8E

claim: EGFP-myosin Va signals are juxtaposed to phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes.
source: EGFP-myosin IIA signals overlapped with phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes (Figure 8E), whereas EGFP-myosin Va signals were juxtaposed to phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 8E

claim: Late endosomes undergo homotypic fusion almost exclusively at the beginning and then switch to heterotypic fusion over time after endocytosis.
source: Late endosomes undergo homotypic fusion almost exclusively at the beginning and then switch to heterotypic fusion over time after endocytosis (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by time course analysis shown in Figure 9A

claim: Actin dynamics are a critical factor for the transition of fusion modes.
source: Given that actin plays a different role in homotypic fusion and heterotypic fusion and that pharmacologic changes in actin dynamics shift the fusion mode as shown above, it is suggested that actin dynamics are a critical factor for the transition of fusion modes.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of actin manipulation on fusion modes

claim: Lysosome biogenesis is regulated by actin dynamics through cofilin downstream of the autotaxin-LPA receptor-Rho-ROCK-LIM kinase pathway in VE cells.
source: Previously, we found that lysosome biogenesis was regulated by actin dynamics through cofilin downstream of the autotaxin–LPA receptor–Rho–ROCK–LIM kinase pathway in VE cells (Koike et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: Treatment with S3 peptide (cofilin activator) fragments lysosomes and reduces phalloidin fluorescence intensity in VE cells.
source: When VE cells were incubated with the S3 peptide, which contains the N-terminal 16 amino acid sequence of cofilin fused to a cell permeation sequence and is used as a competitive inhibitor for LIM kinase and serves as a cofilin activator (Maekawa et al., 1999; Aizawa et al., 2001), lysosomes were fragmented in VE cells and the fluorescence intensity of phalloidin in VE cells was reduced (Koike et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and the authors' previous work

claim: YFP-cofilin shows small punctate staining that colocalizes with phalloidin-positive spots in the x-y plane and extends along the phalloidin signal.
source: We thus focused on cofilin in endosomal fusion in VE cells. YFP-cofilin showed small punctate staining that colocalized with phalloidin-positive spots in the x-y plane and extended along the phalloidin signal (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: Supported by YFP-cofilin localization data shown in Figure 9B and C

claim: Cofilin is slightly more abundant in the apical region of late endosomes, whereas phalloidin signal is stronger in the basal region.
source: When the fluorescence intensity of Alexa 546-phalloidin- and YFP-cofilin-positive filaments was quantitated along the apical-basal axis of late endosomes in zone 2, cofilin was slightly abundant in the apical region, whereas the phalloidin signal was stronger in the basal region (Figure 9D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 9D

claim: Treatment with S3 peptide results in a decrease in radially extended actin filaments in the apical area of zone 2, while actin filaments extending along the apical-basal axis appear unchanged.
source: EGFP-actin on a late endosome showed that treatment of E7.5 whole embryos with the S3 peptide (15 μg/ml) for 24 h resulted in a decrease in radially extended actin filaments in the apical area of zone 2, whereas the actin filaments extending along the apical-basal axis appeared unchanged (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: Treatment with S3 peptide induces faster turnover of actin filaments on late endosomes compared to RV peptide treatment.
source: In addition, a FRAP assay showed that the treatment of S3 peptide induced faster turnover of actin filaments of late endosomes when compared with treatment with the RV peptide (Aizawa et al., 2001), which contains the reverse sequence of cofilin and is used as a negative control (t1/2 = 10.9 s with the S3 peptide, n=9 vs t1/2 = 18.3 s with the RV peptide, n=9; Figure 9E).
evidence: Supported by FRAP assay data shown in Figure 9E

claim: Cofilin distributes with actin filaments on late endosomes and regulates actin dynamics on late endosomes.
source: These results indicate that cofilin distributes with actin filaments on late endosomes and regulates actin dynamics on late endosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the cofilin localization and S3 peptide effects on actin dynamics

claim: S3 peptide strongly inhibits homotypic fusion but not heterotypic fusion.
source: After treatment with the S3 peptide for 24 hr, Alexa 488-transferrin-labeled vesicles were observed by use of time-lapse imaging. When compared with the RV peptide, the S3 peptide strongly inhibited homotypic fusion (Figure 9F) but not heterotypic fusion (Figure 9G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with S3 peptide shown in Figure 9F and G

claim: Spatial differentiation of actin dynamics along the apical-basal direction, partially contributed to by cofilin, may be a critical factor for the transition of fusion modes.
source: These data suggest that spatial differentiation of actin dynamics along the apical-basal direction, partially contributed to by cofilin, may be a critical factor for the transition of fusion modes (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the cofilin distribution and S3 peptide effects

claim: Myosin V facilitates directional transport of late endosomes towards lysosomes along stabilized actin filaments that serve as a rail.
source: We showed that, consistent with the well-known roles of myosin V in trafficking of lysosomes, ER, melanosomes, and synaptic vesicles (Hammer and Sellers, 2011), myosin V facilitates the directional transport of late endosomes towards lysosomes along stabilized actin filaments that serve as a rail (Figure 10).
evidence: This is inferred from the myosin V inhibition data and established knowledge about myosin V function

claim: NM II partially contributes to heterotypic fusion.
source: Moreover, our results indicate that NM II, which is primarily responsible for generating contractile force (Svitkina, 2018), partially contributes to heterotypic fusion.
evidence: Supported by blebbistatin inhibition data and established knowledge about NM II function

claim: In the apical region, late endosomes receive squeezing forces via active actin modification by cofilin and Arp2/3, which leads to homotypic fusion in an explosive mode.
source: In the apical region, late endosomes receive squeezing forces via active actin modification by cofilin and Arp2/3, which leads to homotypic fusion in an explosive mode.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental results, shown in the model in Figure 10

claim: In the basal region, actin is more static and late endosomes receive sliding forces via myosins.
source: In contrast, in the basal region, actin is more static and late endosomes receive sliding forces via myosins.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental results, shown in the model in Figure 10

claim: The hemifusion stage was observed in live cells, providing strong evidence of the hemifusion model.
source: Recently, the hemifusion stage was observed in live cells, providing strong evidence of the hemifusion model (Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: In 'explosive' fusion, the fusion pore expands quickly.
source: In 'explosive' fusion, which is commonly seen in cells, the fusion pore expanded quickly.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies on membrane fusion

claim: In 'bridge' fusion, the pore does not expand; instead, one vesicle gradually shrinks and disappears over time as the result of transfer of its vesicle content into another vesicle.
source: In contrast, in 'bridge' fusion, the pore did not expand; instead, one vesicle gradually shrank and disappeared over time as the result of the transfer of its vesicle content into another vesicle.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies on membrane fusion

claim: In homotypic vacuole fusion in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, vacuole membranes fuse at the vertices instead of a central pore expanding radially.
source: In homotypic vacuole fusion in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, vacuole membranes fused at the vertices instead of a central pore expanding radially, and then a boundary membrane between the two docked vacuoles was released into the vacuole lumen (Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Pore dynamics determine the rate of content mixing and have significant effects on the trafficking efficiency of cargo molecules.
source: Because pore dynamics determine the rate of content mixing, they have significant effects on the trafficking efficiency of cargo molecules.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the relationship between pore dynamics and content mixing

claim: Membrane deformation is generally controlled by membrane-associating proteins and several physical parameters including vesicle volume, membrane area, bending energy, and osmotic energy.
source: Membrane deformation is generally controlled by membrane-associating proteins as well as by several physical parameters including the vesicle volume, membrane area, bending energy, and osmotic energy in cells (Farsad and De Camilli, 2003; Lipowsky, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Actin and its regulating proteins exert physical forces on and cause fluctuation in the membrane, which leads to membrane deformation by modification of physical parameters.
source: Actin and its regulating proteins, via interaction with the membrane, exert physical forces on and cause fluctuation in the membrane, which eventually leads to membrane deformation by modification of the physical parameters (Salbreux et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Assembly of branched actin filaments nucleated by Arp2/3 complex and formins provides pushing forces on the membrane.
source: Actin produces forces in two different manners. First, assembly of branched actin filaments, nucleated from the membrane surface by actin nucleators such as the actin-related protein 2/3 (Arp2/3) complex and formins, provides pushing forces on the membrane (Goley and Welch, 2006; Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Actin generates pulling forces through myosin-driven sliding of actin filaments.
source: Second, actin generates pulling forces through myosin-driven sliding of actin filaments (Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Both pushing and pulling forces play roles in induction of membrane deformation during vesicle fusion.
source: Both forces play roles in induction of membrane deformation during vesicle fusion (Ebrahim et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2015; Uenishi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Polymerization or stabilization of actin enhanced membrane fusion in some experiments but inhibited it in others.
source: For example, polymerization or stabilization of actin enhanced membrane fusion in some experiments but inhibited it in others (reviewed in Eitzen, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article

claim: The regulation mechanisms of vesicle fusion by actin filaments are more complex than previously assumed.
source: These different results imply that the regulation mechanisms of vesicle fusion by actin filaments are more complex than previously assumed.
evidence: This is inferred from the contradictory results in previous studies
